item.title: Services
item.content:encoded:
Six kinds of work

Each project starts with a written scope and a fixed price. The prices below are where most projects start; the scope sets the final figure.

  • Data audit
  • Reporting
  • Demand forecasting
  • Pricing
  • Experiments
  • Customer analysis
From
$6,500
Typical length
3 weeks

Data audit

inventory, cross-system joins, one clean customer table

We list every source your reports depend on, test how well they agree, and fix the joins that break most often.

Most reporting problems start upstream. The CRM counts a customer once per contact, billing counts one per invoice address, and the two never agree on how many customers you have. We find those mismatches before anyone builds a forecast on top of them.

What we check

  • Duplicates and orphaned records
  • Fields that changed meaning over time, like a “region” that was a state until 2021 and a sales territory after
  • Gaps: days, stores or products with no rows at all
  • Refresh times: which report is a day old and which is a week old

What you keep

The checks are plain SQL that runs in your warehouse every night. When one fails, it emails the owner of that source, not us.

What you keep

  • A map of every data source, its owner and its refresh time
  • Row-level checks that run every night
  • One customer table that matches sales, billing and support
  • A written list of what we could not fix, and why
Ask about data audit
From
$8,000
Typical length
4 to 6 weeks

Reporting

defined metrics, one dashboard, a Monday email

One dashboard with fifteen numbers at most, each with a written definition, an owner and the query behind it.

Most companies we meet have forty dashboards and three definitions of revenue. We start by writing down what each number means, then build the smallest report that answers the questions asked in your weekly meeting.

How we build it

  • Interview the five to ten people who use the numbers
  • Write one definition per metric, next to the query that computes it
  • Build the dashboard in Looker Studio, Power BI, Metabase or Tableau, whichever you have
  • Retire the reports nobody opened in the last ninety days

What you keep

  • A metric glossary signed off by your finance lead
  • One dashboard in the tool you already pay for
  • A Monday email with the five numbers that moved most
  • Training for the person who will maintain it
Ask about reporting
From
$12,000
Typical length
6 to 8 weeks

Demand forecasting

weekly forecasts, stock levels, staffing plans

Forecasts by product and location with a range around every number, so buyers can see how sure the model is.

We forecast whatever drives your costs: units, orders, calls or staff hours. Each forecast comes with a back-test, so you can see how the model would have done last year before you trust it this year.

What we model

  • Seasonality and holidays, including the ones that move every year
  • Promotions and price changes, if you have the history
  • Stock-outs, which hide real demand in your sales data
  • New products, using the closest existing ones as a guide

When we say no

With less than eighteen months of history, a forecasting model rarely beats a well-kept spreadsheet. We tell you that in the first week and bill for the first week only.

What you keep

  • A weekly forecast by product and location, 13 weeks ahead
  • An 80% range around every number
  • A back-test against the last two years
  • A plain Python job that reruns every Monday
Ask about demand forecasting
From
$14,000
Typical length
6 to 10 weeks

Pricing

price tests, discount rules, gross margin

We estimate how demand responds to price for each product group, then set prices and discount limits from that.

Most price lists were set once and adjusted by feel. We use your order history to estimate how volume moves when price moves, then set prices where margin is highest without losing the customers you want to keep.

What we usually find

  • Discounts given to customers who would have paid full price
  • Products priced below cost once shipping and returns are counted
  • Price steps that push customers down to the cheaper tier

What you keep

  • Price response estimates by product group
  • Recommended prices, each with its effect on margin
  • Discount rules your sales team can apply without asking
  • A test plan for the changes we are least sure about
Ask about pricing
From
$5,500
Typical length
from 2 weeks per test

Experiments

A/B tests, sample sizes, honest readouts

We design tests that can answer the question, size them before launch and report the result even when it is flat.

Half the tests we are asked to review were too small to detect the effect they were looking for. We fix the sample size and the stop date before launch, so nobody ends a test early because the first week looked good.

What we test

  • Prices, offers and free-shipping thresholds
  • Checkout and sign-up changes
  • Email timing and content
  • Sales scripts, by randomizing which reps use them

What you keep

  • A one-page plan per test: question, metric, sample size, stop date
  • Randomization checks on day one
  • A readout with the effect, its range and what we would do next
  • A log of every test you have run
Ask about experiments
From
$10,000
Typical length
5 to 7 weeks

Customer analysis

segments, churn, lifetime value, who to call first

Segments built from what customers buy and how often, plus a churn score your account managers can use every week.

Segments only help if someone treats each one differently. We build them from order history, not demographics, and agree with your team which action goes with each segment before we hand them over.

Questions we answer

  • Which channel brings the customers who stay longest
  • What the last three orders of a customer who left look like
  • How much you can spend to win back a lapsed account

What you keep

  • Four to six segments with a plain description of each
  • A churn score for every active account, refreshed weekly
  • Lifetime value by acquisition channel
  • The twenty accounts most at risk, in your inbox every Monday
Ask about customer analysis

item.title: About
item.content:encoded:
Five people who show their working

Quillmoor started in 2012, when two statisticians left a grocery chain and a freight company to do the same work for firms that could not hire a data team of their own.

Who you work with

Everyone on your project does the work. There are no juniors learning on your budget.

  • Lead statistician

    Forecasting and experiments. Twelve years in grocery supply chains before Quillmoor.

  • Pricing specialist

    Price response models and discount rules. Previously set prices for a freight carrier.

  • Analytics engineer

    SQL, dbt and warehouses. Builds the checks and jobs you keep after we leave.

  • Reporting lead

    Metric definitions and dashboards. Writes the glossary your finance lead signs.

  • Office manager

    Scheduling, contracts and invoices. The person who answers the phone.

How we charge

  • Fixed price per phase

    You get a price for the diagnostic, then a price for the project. If the scope changes, the price changes in writing before we continue.

  • The diagnostic is credited

    The two-week diagnostic costs $4,800. If you go ahead with the project within three months, we take it off the project price.

  • No retainers

    We invoice monthly against the agreed phases. When the work is done, the invoices stop.

Work we turn down

  • Projects without one person on your side who owns the result
  • Licensing a platform you would have to keep paying for
  • Strategy decks with no numbers behind them
  • Work for two competitors in the same market at the same time
